title: Redefining Strength Podcast
author: Cori Lefkowith
description: A podcast for women struggling with plateaued progress, energy drops, and stalled fat loss despite disciplined efforts. Hosted by Cori Lefkowith, founder of Redefining Strength, the show explores women's health, metabolism, and behavior change through coaching insights and expert conversations.

episodes.title: 10 Ridiculous BLUNT and Honest Truths About Body Recomp
episodes.summary: Cori shares the patterns that quietly undermine progress, from goal-setting to discipline, drawn from nearly two decades of body composition coaching. She explains how to stop the cycle of constantly restarting.

episodes.title: The Worst Cardio For Fat Loss (For Women 40+)
episodes.summary: Cori explains why weight loss and body recomposition are different goals and how piling on steady-state cardio can work against a leaner body. She lays out her muscle-first fat loss approach and the two forms of cardio she uses strategically.

episodes.title: The 7 Laws of Body Recomp After 40 (That Actually Work)
episodes.summary: Seven frameworks Cori has refined over nearly two decades of coaching more than 10,000 women. She argues these principles produce results even in perimenopause when women follow them consistently.

episodes.title: The Scale Is your Worst Frenemy...Here's Why
episodes.summary: Why the number on the scale moves independently of fat loss thanks to water, stress, hormones and inflammation. Cori shares ways to desensitize yourself to the scale and gather context before you weigh in.

episodes.title: Why Menopause Belly Fat Won't Budge (Even When You're Doing Everything Right)
episodes.summary: Cori looks at the hormonal shifts of menopause and why traditional fat-loss tactics fail. A client case study shows how raising calories from 1,000 to 1,650 a day led to both weight loss and restored energy.

episodes.title: The 5 Hidden Metabolism Killers That Are Sabotaging Your Body Recomposition Results
episodes.summary: Five habits that quietly suppress metabolism: clean eating traps, chronic stress, low daily movement, poor sleep and a restrictive mindset. Cori makes the case for muscle as metabolic support.

articles.question: Is cardio bad for fat loss after 40?
articles.metaDescription: Coach Cori Lefkowith of the Redefining Strength Podcast explains why more cardio often backfires for women over 40 and how to use it strategically.
articles.intro: Cardio isn't bad, but using it as your main fat loss tool after 40 usually backfires. On the Redefining Strength Podcast, coach Cori Lefkowith explains that piling on spin classes and treadmill miles helped her look softer, not leaner. Her fix is a muscle-first approach where cardio plays a supporting role instead of the lead.

sections.heading: Weight loss and body recomposition pull in opposite directions
sections.body:
The core mistake Cori describes is treating weight loss and body recomposition as the same goal. They aren't. Weight loss just means the scale goes down, and you can get there by losing muscle along with fat. Body recomposition means you keep or build muscle while losing fat, so you look leaner at the same weight or even a slightly higher one.

Cori is blunt about her own history here. For years she punished herself with spin classes and logged miles on every cardio machine she could find, not because she enjoyed it but because she believed more cardio was the answer. The result was burnout, cravings through the roof, yo-yo dieting and a body that looked softer despite all the work.

The host explains that the approach that drives fast scale loss, big calorie burns and long steady sessions, actively works against the approach that builds a leaner body. Once you see those as two separate targets, the cardio question gets a lot clearer.

quote.text: Weight loss and body recomposition are not the same thing. And the approach that drives one actively works against the other.
quote.speaker: Cori Lefkowith

sections.heading: What long steady cardio does to a woman over 40
sections.body:
After 40, especially through perimenopause, the margin for error shrinks. Recovery takes longer, stress hormones stay elevated more easily, and muscle is harder to hold onto. Cori's point is that endless steady-state cardio adds stress and burns calories without giving your body any reason to keep muscle.

That's the trap she fell into. The extra sessions drove hunger and cravings, which led to overeating and then more restriction, which led to more cardio. Each loop cost a little muscle. Over time the scale might have moved, but the body composition went the wrong way.

She's careful to say this isn't an anti-cardio message. If you love your runs, keep them. The problem is using cardio to dig a bigger calorie hole while hoping it fixes the shape of your body. It doesn't.

sections.heading: The muscle-first order of operations
sections.body:
Cori's system puts strength training and nutrition first, then layers cardio on top strategically. In practice that looks like:

- **Lift to keep and build muscle.** Muscle is what makes you look lean and what supports your metabolism as you age. It has to be the priority, not the thing you squeeze in after cardio.
- **Eat enough protein and enough food.** Her related episodes make the same point repeatedly: under-eating stalls results. In one client case she shares, raising intake from 1,000 to 1,650 calories a day produced both fat loss and more energy.
- **Use cardio with a purpose.** She describes two forms of cardio she uses on purpose inside a muscle-first plan. The goal is to support recovery, conditioning and health rather than to chase a calorie number.

The host explains that when training and nutrition work together instead of against each other, cardio stops sabotaging your hard work and starts helping it.

quote.text: This isn't an anti-cardio approach. It's about understanding what different types of cardio actually do to your results.
quote.speaker: Cori Lefkowith

sections.heading: How to tell if your cardio is hurting your results
sections.body:
A few signs from Cori's own story are worth checking against your week:

- You're doing cardio you don't enjoy because you think you have to.
- Cravings and hunger climb on the days you do more of it.
- You keep restarting diets and feel constantly burnt out.
- The scale moves a little but you don't look any leaner in photos.

If that sounds familiar, the answer isn't more effort. It's reordering the effort. Keep the cardio you love, cut the punishment sessions, and put the freed-up energy into lifting and eating enough to recover from it.

keyTakeaways: Weight loss and body recomposition are different goals, and chasing the first with lots of cardio can cost you the second.
Steady-state cardio done for calorie burn tends to raise hunger and stress while giving your body no reason to keep muscle.
Put strength training and adequate protein first, then add cardio for a specific purpose.
You don't have to quit the runs or rides you enjoy; just stop using cardio as a fat loss crutch.
Constant burnout, cravings and restarting diets are signs the cardio-first approach is working against you.

faq.q: How much cardio should a woman over 40 do for fat loss?
faq.a: Cori doesn't prescribe a fixed number. Her advice is to make lifting and nutrition the foundation and to use cardio strategically, keeping the sessions you enjoy and dropping the ones you only do to burn calories.

faq.q: Does walking count as cardio for body recomposition?
faq.a: Low-intensity movement like walking is easy to recover from and doesn't drive the hunger and stress that hard steady-state sessions can. It fits well into a muscle-first plan as daily activity.

faq.q: Why do I look softer even though I'm losing weight?
faq.a: That's usually a sign you're losing muscle along with fat. Cori describes exactly this happening to her during her heavy cardio years, and the fix was shifting to strength training and eating enough to support it.
